title: The Socinians' chief motive: certain foreknowledge would make God's earnest exhortations pointless
source_text: XIX. Sed qui hodie contendunt in Deo non esse certam praescientiam futurorum contingentium, eo praecipue moventur quod, si ea quae libere homines facturi sunt Deus certo praevidet, & quidem ab aeterno, non potest, ut ipsi existimant, homines serio monere, hortari, atque obtestari, ut convertantur atq; resipiscant. Ad quid enim opus est sollicite aliquem hortari atque compellere, ut faciat id quod pro comperto habes illum esse facturum; aut cui bono uti sollicitatione, & obtestatione multa, apud eum quem exploratum tibi est nihil eorum quae rogas facturum esse?
pass_a_gloss: But those who today contend that there is not in God a certain foreknowledge of future contingents, are chiefly moved by this that, if God certainly foresees those things which men are going to do freely, and that from eternity, he cannot, as they think, seriously admonish, exhort, and adjure men, that they be converted and repent. For to what purpose is there need anxiously to exhort and urge someone, to do that which you hold for ascertained he will do; or for what good to use solicitation, and much adjuration, with him of whom it is explored to you that he will do none of those things which you ask?
pass_b_english: Those who today maintain that God has no certain foreknowledge of future contingents are moved chiefly by this. If God foresees with certainty, and from eternity, what human beings will freely do, then in their view he cannot seriously warn, exhort and implore them to turn and repent.

'What need is there,' they ask, 'to exhort and press someone earnestly to do what you know for sure he will do? And what is the good of much pleading and imploring with someone who, as you well know, will do none of the things you ask?'

choices.why: The Schools' term for future events without a necessary and determinate cause; kept as a technical term.
